title: Surdas's single line
hook: a single line: leave the company of those turned away from the Lord (Sarang, Surdas, ang 1253)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Parmanand asked what all the listening was for: hear, then do. Today, a teaching so short it's one line.

Some parts of the Guru Granth Sahib run on for pages: long ballads, rows and rows of saloks. Then, in Raag Sarang, on the same Ang as yesterday's hymn, there's the name Surdas, and with it a single line. No verses after it, no story around it. It sits there like a note pinned to a door on the way out. Somebody decided one line was worth keeping, and it carries Surdas's name.
screen: `PAGES OF BALLADS AND SALOKS.` → `A HEADING: SURDAS.` → `ONE LINE, PINNED TO THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here is the line, in paraphrase: O mind, leave the company of those who have turned away from the Lord. The key word is bemukh: one whose face is turned the other way. Not a cartoon villain. Someone whose whole attention points away from God. Who was this Surdas? Tradition tells more than one story about the name, and the Granth doesn't settle it. What it gives is the line, and where it puts it. Just before it stands a hymn headed with Guru Arjan's mark and the name Surdas together, about the Lord's people who live close to the Lord. So one page holds both sides of the same idea: the company that draws you near, and the company that turns you away. Now the hard part, because a line like this can be misused. It isn't a license to look down on anyone. Sikh teaching puts great weight on sangat, the company you keep, because company shapes a mind the way water shapes a stone, slowly and without asking. The line talks to the mind, not to the neighbors. It doesn't say: judge them. It says: notice what you're sitting in. People, voices, feeds and habits: some turn the face toward what matters, and some turn it away a little more each day, so slowly it's easy to miss. Surdas doesn't argue the case. One line, and the choosing is left to you.
screen: `O MIND, LEAVE THE COMPANY OF THE TURNED-AWAY.` · `BEMUKH: THE FACE TURNED THE OTHER WAY.` · `TWO SIDES ON ONE PAGE.` · `SANGAT SHAPES A MIND, NOT A LICENSE TO JUDGE.` · then, large: `ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Let the last few days pass in front of you: the people, the voices in your ears, the screens, the conversations. Without judging anyone, notice which left your face turned toward what you care about, and which turned it away. If you pray, breathe out Waheguru and rest in the good company you found.
Bemukh. One whose face is turned away from the Lord: Surdas's single line, kept whole, telling the mind to leave that company.
Your line: one line. Some teachings fit on a note pinned to a door. That's day seven hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of sangat, the company of those who remember God, as something that shapes a person, and gather in the gurdwara partly to keep that company; Surdas's line is read in that light.

chat.says: Surdas says leave the company of the turned-away. So should I judge my friends?
options: No. It speaks to your own mind: notice which company turns your face to God.
Yes. It tells you to cut off anyone who doesn't pray, and say why.
Yes. It means people who turn away from God can never be forgiven.
chat.meaning: The line talks to the mind, not the neighbors: sangat, the company you keep, shapes you slowly. It's no license to judge anyone.
